author: Brian Hioe
title: What is the Future of KMT-TPP Cooperation?
content:
THE KMT AND TPP’S future cooperation–or lack thereof–has increasingly become questioned in the course of elections.

The TPP would seem to be at a crossroads. The party was originally built as a vehicle for party founder Ko Wen-je’s bid for the presidency. But Ko is likely to return to jail soon on corruption charges over accepting bribes to expand the floor area of the Core Pacific City Mall.

With Huang Kuo-chang as the party’s acting chair, the party has lost many of its previous visible political figures. As many were Ko associates, it is possible that Huang drove them out of the party in his quest to maintain power of the party, with Huang having historically not been part of the TPP before suddenly taking leadership. This occurs even as Huang publicly vows fidelity to Ko and his ideals.

Likewise, though the TPP could have controlled the balance of power in the legislature by playing the DPP and KMT off from each other and, in that way, becoming the “kingmaker” within the Legislative Yuan, this has not occurred. Instead, the TPP has simply sided with the KMT on most policy initiatives–even highly controversial ones, such as drastically slashing the government budget, freezing the Constitutional Court, or expanding legislative powers.

This apparent lack of awareness that the party’s best interests were served by counter-balancing between the KMT and DPP, in line with the party’s claim to be beyond traditional partisan divisions in Taiwanese politics, is probably due to the fact that the majority of its politicians come from pan-Blue backgrounds. It may have been path dependency that caused the TPP to become overly reliant on the KMT.

ONE NOTES that party chair Huang Kuo-chang originally planned to run for New Taipei mayor, given that he was formerly a legislator of Xizhi. But Huang backed out in favor of Lee Shu-chuan of the KMT when polling results showed a stronger performance by Lee. That Lee is struggling against Su Chiao-hui of the DPP may make it sting that the KMT passed over Huang.

There are some places where the KMT has declined to run a candidate, but instead decided to back a TPP one. Hsinchu city mayor Ann Kao, for example, is still often regarded as part of the TPP despite technically being an independent, having departed the party after facing corruption charges that she was later acquitted of. Kao is running with the backing of the KMT and TPP, though she has often used the KMT’s blue when campaigning.

Chiayi City is another constituency where a TPP candidate is running with the endorsement of the KMT and TPP. However, the TPP candidate there, Chiang Chi-kai, recently courted controversy after being caught on camera urinating in public on a bush while on the campaign trail.

Still, splits opened up between the KMT and TPP in Zhubei, the administrative capital of Hsinchu County. There, the KMT has nominated Wu Hsu-chih, while the TPP has nominated Chiu Chen-yuan, but neither candidate agreed to back out in favor of the other.

As such, this led KMT chair Cheng Li-wun to declare an end to political cooperation between the KMT and TPP in Hsinchu County as a whole. This has not prevented Chiang Wan-an and pan-Blue commentator Jaw Shaw-kong from making public appearances with Chiu, in what has been questioned as potentially violating party discipline. That both party heavyweights have been willing to break from party discipline may reflect that Cheng’s grip over the KMT is quite weak at present.

Oppositely, in Hualien, the TPP county branch chair, Chang Tien-min, broke from party discipline to endorse independent Chang Chun rather than KMT nominee Yu Shu-chen. Chang has criticized Yu as beholden to KMT legislative caucus chair Fu Kun-chi’s political dynasty, which has historically dominated Hualien.

IN EVALUATING the current state of TPP-KMT relations, then, one sees cooperation in some districts while open competition in others. It is generally thought that current KMT chair Cheng Li-wun does not favor cooperating with the TPP, seeing it as splitting votes from the KMT and being an unnecessary collaborator, while others in the KMT, such as Chiang Wan-an, cling to the TPP as part of an attempt to rally votes.

Indeed, in the meantime, with days until the vote, the TPP’s alignment with Chiang Wan-an has strengthened in what increasingly looks like a desperate attempt by Chiang to fend off challenger Puma Shen. Chiang appeared at the TPP’s rally last Saturday in front of City Hall and was later gifted a copy of the Diamond Sutra and a personal letter by Ko. Ko has also increasingly leaned into attacks on Shen.

Likewise, Huang Kuo-chuang has been given new mileage by Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, who has taken to frequent public appearances with not only Huang, but streamer Holger Chen–another figure often associated with the TPP. If Huang’s leadership of the TPP is ever challenged, his claim to power may increasingly become his close relationship with the KMT, even if that further erodes the difference between the TPP and KMT. Some KMT politicians, too, are not happy with Chiang, seeing as his alliance with the TPP could cost the KMT seats on the city council.

Not all in the TPP have gone along with Ko’s attacks on Shen. Former legislator Huang Shan-shan, for example, gifted Shen signed copies of her book. In turn, Shen has touted these gifts in campaigning, so as to signal non-partisanship. It is to be seen whether Huang is contemplating jumping ship from the TPP and toward alignment with Shen’s “Ocean Current”.

The TPP’s days, after all, may be limited if the party continues to be led by Huang and if its spiritual leader, Ko, will eventually end up behind bars. And a number of the TPP’s politicians, including Huang, had political careers before their later alignment with Ko out of political expedience–they did not join the TPP out of personal loyalty to Ko, and if the TPP no longer serves their interests, they may bolt. This is to be seen.

The TPP’s future as a political party is broadly up in the air, then. Apart from the question of the party’s current leadership, given how closely the party has aligned with the KMT on controversial initiatives in past years makes it risk being a “little blue” party whose main difference from the KMT is being smaller than it.

If so, the TPP perhaps faces a doom not so different than that faced by the NPP–the other major third party in Taiwanese politics in the past decade–which eventually could not distinguish itself from the DPP besides being a “little green” party smaller than it and so was eventually largely absorbed into it. So, too, may be the fate of the TPP if it is unable to prove its value to the pan-Blue camp as a smaller party.

The party’s one major rally in Taipei in the past week on last Saturday, had respectable numbers, bringing out a number of young people, sufficient to prove that KMT politicians who struggle to appeal to young people may still benefit by association with the TPP. But that still does not fix the question of the TPP’s long-term future.

author: Brian Hioe
title: The Referendum Nobody is Talking About
content:
THE ONLY REFERENDUM question that will be asked of the general public during the vote that takes place on Saturday will be on nuclear energy. Specifically, the public will be asked about phasing out current government policy on enacting a nuclear-free homeland.

The referendum question proves ironic. For one, this will be the fourth time that the Taiwanese public has been asked about nuclear energy in a referendum in eight years. All of these referendums on nuclear energy were proposed by pro-nuclear advocates.

Likewise, one wonders if the referendum is even necessary at this juncture. The Lai administration has long since reversed course on nuclear energy to allow for restarts. Plans to restart the No. 2 and No. 3 nuclear reactors were submitted by state-run power utility Taipower to the Atomic Energy Commission earlier this year.

The Lai administration reversing course on the DPP’s opposition to nuclear energy, a plank of the party that dates back to democratization, is primarily due to two reasons. One is concern about how Taiwan would maintain a stable power supply in the event of a Chinese invasion or blockade, seeing as Taiwan is highly reliant on shipments of liquefied natural gas for its energy supply.

Taiwan has a limited supply of liquefied natural gas that it can rely on if supplies are cut off, which has led the Lai administration to contemplate the possibility of emergency restarts in the event of a crisis. The Lai administration has been willing to risk controversy in the past, coming into conflict with environmentalist groups, by building LNG receiving terminals even when they threaten coral reefs and maritime diversity.

The second reason as to why the Lai administration would reverse course on nuclear energy, however, is because of concern from the international community about how Taiwan intends to maintain semiconductor manufacturing to continue to fuel the AI boom without nuclear energy. Indeed, nuclear energy was never a silver bullet for Taiwan’s energy needs, constituting 1.2% to 4% by the time it was phased out in May 2025. But international business concerns came to discuss nuclear energy as though nuclear energy would solve all of Taiwan’s energy needs.

The KMT has hit out at what it claims to be the Lai administration’s hypocrisy in reversing course on nuclear energy, while still calling for the referendum. The Lai administration took a political risk in reversing course on what historically has been a pan-Green platform and it was, surprisingly, able to get the pan-Green camp to accept the decision, not necessarily because it did so from a position of power, but because of rising concerns about invasion scenarios and how to maintain social operations in the event of no LNG shipments.

Yet one notes the KMT could have taken action using its current control of the legislature, which dates from 2024, to try to prevent the Lai administration from phasing out nuclear energy. The recommissioning process for nuclear reactors will probably take several years, when the KMT was in a position to have taken more decisive action against it. The KMT does not necessarily need to hold a referendum either when it has the majority in the legislature when it votes alongside the TPP and could simply press certain legal measures into law through this majority. The KMT itself probably strategically decided to allow for the nuclear phase-out to occur because it realized it could later leverage on the campaign promise to restore nuclear energy for electoral ends.

Moreover, if the Lai administration has already reversed course on nuclear energy, it proves a question as to why the referendum is still necessary–except for that the KMT hopes to benefit electorally from it. More generally, the KMT hopes to repeat its successes in the 2018 local elections, in which it was able to successfully leverage on a series of nine referendum questions asked of the Taiwanese public to win district elections across Taiwan.

Indeed, one notes that the KMT and its pan-Blue ally, the TPP, had previously pushed for other referendum questions to be on the ballot beyond simply nuclear energy. Apart from the issue of nuclear energy, the KMT and TPP had also pushed for a referendum that would institute caning for serious crimes, and a referendum to call for allocation of fines from traffic violations to local governments in order to improve traffic safety.

There was no previous social demand for caning, which the KMT claimed would be used for crimes such as sexual assault, large-scale fraud, and child abuse, and would serve as a deterrent to such crimes by setting a social example. This would be in line with the KMT’s historic support for the use of capital punishment in Taiwan, which the KMT claims deters violent crimes by setting an example.

The KMT previously claimed that violent crimes were on the rise in Taiwan because of the Lai administration’s refusal to implement capital punishment, depicting a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling that narrowed the scope of its application as having abolished capital punishment, and calling for a referendum in favor of capital punishment last year. This would be a claim perhaps not unlike how the KMT has continued to push for its current pro-nuclear referendum despite that the Lai administration is in fact in favor of nuclear reactors. But the Central Election Commission refused to allow the referendum to occur, seeing as capital punishment is still on the books.

Indeed, one notes that most countries in the world that implement caning are former British colonies or countries with Sharia law. Instituting caning would result in a wave of international mockery of Taiwan on human rights grounds. To this extent, allocating funds from traffic violations to traffic safety does not require a national referendum, but could simply be passed as a measure by the KMT-controlled legislature.

In this sense, both referendums were blocked by the Central Election Commission, even if the nuclear referendum was still allowed. For its part, the KMT remains committed at least to the notion of a caning referendum, and claims that it will attempt to pass laws to this effect in the legislature–even as a caning referendum might fall afoul of international human rights conventions that Taiwan voluntarily ratified under the Ma Ying-jeou administration.

And yet with the DPP itself having reversed course on nuclear energy in a manner that runs contrary to how the KMT has attempted to depict it, it is possible that the DPP has taken the wind out of the KMT’s sails when it comes to its pro-nuclear referendum. Moreover, one notes that compared to 2018, there is relatively little social discussion of the referendum in an election cycle dominated by Puma Shen’s “Ocean Current.”

This perhaps returns to the fact that the KMT did not actually collect signatures with the public and campaign for the referendum to take place, building momentum around the issue and raising publicity for it, but simply did so by passing the referendum using its current majority in the legislature. If this results in little publicity for the referendum and fails to benefit in district elections, perhaps the KMT will be seen as frivolous for yet again attempting to make the public vote on nuclear energy in the belief that this will help its election chances.

Indeed, indications are that the KMT has started to realize its failure to emphasize the referendum in campaigning. Reportedly, this could be one of the reasons why the KMT has switched to attacks on solar energy in the final stage of campaigning, rather than championing nuclear energy. This is to be seen. Either way, one notes that the KMT’s advocacy of nuclear energy is not based on scientific rationale but primarily based on appeals to past history, during which nuclear energy constituted more than 50% of the energy mix, the KMT held sole power, and Taiwan’s economy saw high growth. The claim, then, is that returning to a traditional form of power would lead to the return of such economic prosperity.

author: Brian Hioe
title: How Can We Explain the Rise of Puma Shen’s “Ocean Current”?
content:
MANY COMMENTATORS have been at odds in explaining the meteoric rise of Puma Shen as a DPP candidate in Taipei.

Regardless of the outcome of the race, it seems that Shen will have a political future. It is self-evident at this point that Shen is on track to be the best-performing DPP mayoral candidate in the 30 years since Chen Shui-bian–who, after all, later became Taiwan’s president.

At the same time, it was expected by few that Shen would become not only a household name, but electrify the elections across all of Taiwan. The effect of what has been termed the “Ocean Current” has powerfully affected races across Taiwan, boosting the DPP’s chances in Taiwan as a whole.

Races which were previously thought to be close, such as in New Taipei, may potentially be tipped in the direction of the DPP. Specifically, in New Taipei, Lee Shu-chuan of the KMT was already struggling against Su Chiao-hui of the DPP, probably due to a lack of experience as a campaigner even if he was known as a strong administrator.

In this sense, even if Puma Shen does not win in Taipei, it is possible that the DPP still benefits elsewhere. Puma Shen has, then–to quote Nathan Batto–become something of a “public resource” for the DPP in that he has been called on to campaign for DPP politicians nationwide. Each of those politicians benefits from public appearances with Shen, even if Shen is, of course, only running in Taipei.

The ubiquity of Puma Shen’s “Ocean Current” imagery in urban spaces, then, reminds something of past social movement uprisings in Taiwan. During the course of the 2014 Sunflower Movement, one could readily identify on the subway, on streets, in cafes, who was supportive of the movement–these were usually young people who had ribbons, flags, and other signifiers of the movement attached to their bags, or in the form of stickers on laptops and phones.

Now, it is the ubiquitous Ocean Current ribbon that appears everywhere. To give a sense of how enthusiastic the public is about the Ocean Current phenomenon, DAYBREAK–the cafe that New Bloom runs in Wanhua–is located outside of a DPP city councilor’s office. For merch distribution that starts at 7:00 PM, a line regularly forms at 2:30 PM.

It is possible that the Shen campaign has managed to tap into the merch-crazy impulses of Taiwanese society, in line with Shen’s anime otaku stylings. After all, the urge to collect is now such that main convenience stores–that ubiquitous institution of Taiwanese society–have begun selling anime merchandise or offering raffle lottery tickets for limited-edition merchandise.

Or it could be Shen’s public image. Shen has managed to depict himself as policy-crazy, an otaku anime nerd, in such a way as to convince the public that he is an expert on public policy, tapping into the fact that he was already known as a researcher of Chinese disinformation strong on data analytics.

But at a time in which Japanese anime, manga, and video games are highly popular among young people, Shen has also managed to use his otaku self-depiction to avoid a technocratic image–rather, his interest in anime, manga, and video games has made him relatable to members of the public in a way that his competitor, Chiang Wan-an struggles to–even if it has resulted in some odd moments such as Shen claiming to the media that Neon Genesis Evangelion, the apotheosis of Japanese animated postmodernism, has taught him lessons about responsible urban governance. But by contrast, one is hard-pressed to name any of Chiang’s hobbies off the top of one’s head,

Yet it also does not seem to be merely Shen’s stylings that have made him popular–indeed, something that the KMT failed to understand after its defeat in 2016 in the wake of the Sunflower Movement, somehow seeing the movement as a successful tactical innovation of the DPP. Rather, one must take into account the contents of Shen’s political message.

One has sometimes seen the comparison between Shen and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, as a left-wing youth candidate whose victory against high odds attracted global attention. But even if Shen’s message has been less about socioeconomic inequality and more about competent and good governance, perhaps Taipei voters are simply tired of nepotistic governance from the usual KMT politicians who usually dominate Taipei–one notes that almost all of Taipei’s KMT mayoral candidates in past decades have hailed from powerful political families, whether that be Ma Ying-jeou, Hau Lung-bin, Sean Lien, or Chiang himself–after all, the self-proclaimed great-grandson of Chiang Kai-shek. The heirs of political dynasties are increasingly perceived by the public as arrogant, in seeing themselves above the everyday person. It is not for nothing that Chiang has repeatedly been hit by controversies revolving around his failure to pick up some gift from a temple.

Shen’s skill as a politician has been notably in his strong capacity for oration–in making the details of a policy proposal engaging, rather than boring in such a way as to alienate voters. It is a noted trend among post-Sunflower Movement politicians such as Shen to try to engage with the concrete details of policy, rather than merely empty slogans.

In the past, this led candidates to try to refrain from empty campaign slogans on election banners and instead have QR codes leading to a website about one’s platform. Or to give speeches that did not consist purely of a Manichaean narrative of good and evil between one and one’s political opponent and empty slogans. Yet the public generally tended to tune out of boring speeches ground in policy details–what Shen has done, however, is through his strong oration been able to make such speeches engaging.

Shen, then, has managed to combine the desire of progressive post-Sunflower candidates for a policy-oriented focus with a dynamic style of political engagement. Perhaps it was this that the public was looking for.

To this extent, while Shen was mostly known for political stances that were tough on China before his current burst of popularity, he has refrained from this in order to focus on local policy issues. Local elections, after all, are primarily about local issues, while national issues pertain to cross-strait policy. But part of his appeal among young people is probably precisely that he is known for his pro-Taiwan stances–and yet this clearly does not have to be his main source of appeal, but can remain implicit, in line with the views of the “natural independence” generation who naturally sees itself as culturally and politically independent from China, as a form of positive identity, without needing to ground its identity as founded on a “negative identity” that is defined in opposition to China.

And yet, if the Ocean Current reminds so much of past social movement uprisings in Taiwan, not only in the ubiquity of its messaging, but in how it has electrified society, perhaps this should not surprise. Social movement uprisings have often fed into elections, whether that is with the Sunflower Movement of 2014 and its relation to the DPP’s unprecedented presidential and legislative victory in 2016. Such transitions from movement politics to electoral politics would be attempts to capture the dynamic energy of movements into a more structural, sustainable form.

Notably, the Ocean Current was preceded by not only the Bluebird Movement in 2024, but the Great Recall Movement in 2025. The latter movement, as the historic attempt to recall all KMT legislators, was already an attempt to steer the spontaneous energy of the Bluebird Movement into electoral politics. Likewise, the Bluebird Movement itself was partly prompted by anger over Shen’s being beaten by KMT legislators in a scuffle in the Legislative Yuan–proving an early show of his popularity. And even if the Great Recall Movement was ultimately unsuccessful, its energy did not dissipate entirely, but clearly laid the groundwork for the later Ocean Current. It may not be so surprising, in this light, that one would see what could be read as a movement mobilization on the scale of these preceding two movements around Shen, with this momentum not having appeared out of nothing.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Shen Reaches Across Political Aisle, Chiang Hits Out at Solar Panels in Second Mayoral Policy Presentation
content:
THE SECOND and last Taipei mayoral policy presentation was held on Saturday, November 21st. The major candidates are Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Though a number of fringe candidates also presented, this article will focus on Shen and Chiang. The policy presentation was not a formal debate, in that there were no opportunities provided for candidates to question each other. Though the Shen campaign had pressed for further debates beyond the one formal debate that has taken place to date, the Chiang campaign is thought to be more reluctant.

Shen was the first to go. Shen first began by stressing bipartisanship, mentioning how Huang Shan-shan of the TPP had gifted him two signed copies of her book. To this extent, Shen raised how he hoped to learn from the experiences of past Taipei mayors, regardless of political affiliation. Indeed, non-partisanship has been something that Shen has been at odds to emphasize in past days, as a DPP candidate running in traditionally blue Taipei.

Shen proved more combative than in other debates or policy presentations, however. Shen criticized the Taipei city government for being insufficiently responsive to the public, as observed in its slow response to child abuse cases, a building collapse in Dazhi, and a food poisoning incident that killed six people in 2024. author: Brian Hioe
title: Chiang Stresses Accomplishments, Shen Calls for Shifts in First Mayoral Policy Presentation
content:
IN THE FIRST Taipei mayoral policy presentation held on November 14th, six mayoral candidates presented their visions for Taipei. For the sake of brevity, this article will only focus on Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, as the two serious candidates in the race, apart from fringe candidates.

Shen was the first to present in the policy presentation. Shen began by referencing a meeting he had with former Taipei city councilor Chen Chien-chih of the KMT, so as to depict himself as bipartisan and willing to meet with the opposition. In the wake of the meeting, Chiang scrambled to hold a similar meeting with Chen. As his campaign has emphasized positive campaigning rather than partisan attacks on opponents, Shen praised the achievements of prior Taipei mayors–most of whom have been KMT.

Shen then turned toward proposals for urban policy. Shen called attention to the life needs of Taipei residents, such as how commuting reduced the amount of time that they had for exercise or taking care of themselves. Shen stated that he had collected such opinions from soapbox speeches and other means of directly engaging with the public. As such, Shen stated that because he had found that members of the public prefer exercising outside, he would set up exercise stations in parks and riversides, with shower stations so that people could continue going about their day while integrating exercise without needing to return home to freshen up.

Shen, too, would continue efforts to integrate transportation networks in the greater Taipei area using TPass, and take advantage of unused space such as under Civic Boulevard, following models from other cities. Shen stressed a campaign platform to increase the amount of greenery in Taipei, noting that his research had shown that Taipei residents were greatly concerned about the decreasing number of trees in the city, with a pledge to ensure that residents could see trees from their homes. Likewise, the continuation of the Culture Coin program would provide stimulation for young and old alike, allowing them to enjoy cultural activities subsidized by the government. To this extent, the government would provide training for AI tools for young people, middle-aged, and the elderly, as well as mental health services, building on programs that already exist. To deal with issues regarding aging homes, the government would publicize data about structures and simplify processes for urban renewal.

On the other hand, Chiang Wan-an stressed his accomplishments as Taipei mayor, seeing as he is the incumbent. At the same time, one notes some overlap between his and Chiang’s proposals. Chiang also emphasized that the integration of transportation networks in the greater Taipei area through TPass would continue, through the reduction of prices. Chiang stressed efforts to make roads near schools safer. Chiang, too, stressed successes in making the entrances to metro stations safer, addressing Taipei’s longstanding reputation for poor pedestrian safety.

Again, stressing his record, Chiang touted successes in providing housing subsidies and subsidies for young families. Chiang also praised the record of his predecessor, Ko Wen-je, in what might have been an effort to reach out to TPP supporters, in building social housing and stated that efforts to increase the amount of social housing in Taipei would continue. Chiang also stressed urban renewal, and then touted subsidies provided by the city government for renovation of housing infrastructure, such as paying for the installation of elevators in buildings, as well as assistance that the city had provided to young parents in providing childcare services, or educational opportunities. In a time of a declining birthrate and in which the number of pets outnumbers children, Chiang pledged to increase social services available to pets.

Chiang also brought up AI, specifically linking this to education, and how AI had been integrated into education. English education was a point of focus for Taiwan, along with science education. To appeal to public servants and teachers, Chiang brought up benefits that his mayoral administration had provided to them, suggesting that care for them improved social services as a whole. To appeal to Indigenous and Hakka voters, Chiang cited efforts by his administration to provide for cultural education.

If Chiang mostly coasted off of his accomplishments as mayor and offered a rather bland package of policies, he still managed well enough in the policy presentation. Shen, on the other hand, probably had the stronger public speaking skills and more distinctive platform, through an emphasis on collecting data on the needs of Taipei residents and crafting policy accordingly. Nevertheless, one notes some overlap between his policy platform and that of Chiang’s. In this sense, the Taipei mayoral policy presentation–as with the Taipei mayoral debate before it–likely will not have a substantial impact on campaigning, if Chiang managed well enough and Shen did not sharply distinguish himself enough from Chiang.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Taichung Mayoral Debate Emphasizes International Prestige
content:
THE TAICHUNG MAYORAL debate was held on November 17th. The two primary candidates were Ho Hsin-chun of the DPP and Johnny Chiang of the KMT. Ho was first to speak, followed by Chiang.

Ho began by criticizing Chiang and outgoing KMT Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen for attempting to convince the public falsely that the DPP would end subsidies to the elderly. Ho then went on to point to Taichung’s growing role as Taiwan’s second-largest city, but that issues involving traffic jams and poor transportation infrastructure were increasingly visible. This included addressing congestion on highways, as well as finishing the MRT Blue Line, and increasing international links through the Taichung International Airport. Likewise, Ho stated that there needed to be more subsidies and government policy to assist young people and provide them with opportunities. Ho suggested that the KMT administration of Taichung had stalled progress, but that, in government, she would be able to allow for coordination between the central government and local government.

Johnny Chiang stressed his love of Taichung, as well as his successes in the past in winning international productions to visit Taichung to film. Chiang stated that he was motivated to improve Taichung in running for office, and that he hoped for Taichung to become an internationally esteemed city. author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Passes Cash Handouts, Leans into Attacks on Solar Energy Before Elections
content:
THE KMT PASSED a 20,000 NT cash handout to the general public yesterday in the legislature, shortly before elections. This would continue a familiar tactic of the party–to distribute cash handouts to the public in order to affect election outcomes. The TPP, unusually, broke from the KMT when it came to the cash handout at the last minute, but because insufficient DPP legislators were present in the legislature, it still passed.

Indeed, this has proven to be a useful electoral tactic in the past. While President Lai Ching-te called for opposition to the cash hand-outs, one notes that on other occasions the DPP first resisted cash hand-outs and then pivoted toward trying to take credit for the move after seeing that it was popular with the public. At other times, it has been the DPP itself that sought to move for cash hand-outs with the claim that this was distributing the dividends of Taiwan’s AI windfall to the public.

At the same time, one notes that, both last year and this year, the KMT pushed a drastic, far-reaching set of cuts to the government budget. This includes not only the defense budget but social services. While the KMT has claimed that such budgets were necessary for fiscal balance, the cuts it currently calls for would be at the expense of social services.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Trilateral Meeting Between Xi, Trump, and Putin Results In Little Substance, But Taiwan Should Remain Cautious
content:
THE TRILATERAL SUMMIT between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping that was held earlier this week resulted in little of substance. Nevertheless, the summit should raise risks for Taiwan, seeing as Taiwan could stand to have its freedoms traded off through Trump’s unpredictable dealmaking.

Indeed, if the summit was intended to harken back to Yalta in the dealmaking that ended World War II, it did not have such significance. The three leaders came to an agreement about peace and nuclear disarmament, as well as boosting fuel production.

Ukraine came up indirectly, and even as Russian strikes on Ukraine continued during the meeting and its talk of peace, no agreement was made between the US and Russia on it. As reflected in the eventual readout, during the meeting, Trump lashed out at the International Criminal Court in what might be read as a conciliatory gesture to Putin, seeing as he is wanted by the court.

It may be fortunate for Taiwan, then–as with Ukraine–that it did not come up in the meeting. It is thought that the possibility of Trump taking some stance on Taiwan that would have signed away its freedoms to China was lessened by allegations against Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that he was involved in an affair with a Chinese spy. author: Brian Hioe
title: Nuclear Energy Debate Sees Dehumanizing Language, Personal Attacks by KMT Nuclear Advocate
content:
THE THIRD POLICY debate on nuclear energy held for the referendum this election was held on November 16th. The debate has drawn attention because of the many colorful comments by pro-nuclear advocate Huang Shih-chiu, a former assistant to ex-KMT chair Hung Hsiu-chu who later came to work for Terry Gou. Huang was debating electronics expert and anti-nuclear group spokesperson Shen Pei-lin. The debate took place in two rounds of exchanges.

Huang attacked the DPP with the claim that it advocated for green energy only because of corruption–a longstanding claim that the KMT has circulated in order to cast doubt on green energy development in Taiwan. In this, Huang lashed out at DPP politicians ranging from President Lai Ching-te to former chair Wu Nai-teh, and former legislator Lai Pin-yu, making personal attacks on all of them. Huang claimed that nuclear energy was an internationally accepted standard by the US and other countries and that Taiwan would be viewed with skepticism by the US if it did not adopt nuclear energy.

At the same time, Huang lashed out at the DPP for hypocrisy, seeing as the Lai administration has long since reversed course on nuclear energy. That the Lai administration is now willing to allow for nuclear restarts, as a result of Taiwan’s energy needs in the event of an invasion and the need for energy to fuel the AI boom, has taken much of the steam out of

author: Brian Hioe
title: Lo Ta-yu Stokes Controversy for Comments Lashing Out at Pan-Green Camp, Misogyny
content:
ICONIC SINGER-SONGWRITER Lo Ta-yu provoked controversy earlier this month after comments in an interview lashing out at the pan-Green camp.

Some of Lo’s comments strayed into misogyny. Specifically, Lo lashed out at former President Tsai Ing-wen and current Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim for being unmarried women who do not have children. Lo claimed that this marked their unsuitability for public office, in that not having children meant that they did not have a stake in the future of Taiwanese society.

Such claims have been used against Tsai and Hsiao in the past, as a form of misogyny directed at female politicians. Indeed, such claims have also occurred from within the pan-Green camp. Veteran independence activist and entrepreneur Koo Kwang-ming, who died in 2023 at age 96, previously made comments suggesting that the ROC military should not be led by a woman who wears a skirt, and suggesting that Tsai not having children made her unsuitable to lead the DPP. Koo suggested, then, that Tsai should step aside to become “mother of the nation” and allow a male leader–his preference being current president Lai Ching-te–to take power. Koo backed Lai in his unsuccessful challenge against Lai in 2020 for the DPP’s presidential nomination.

Nevertheless, one notes that frequent public scrutiny of female politicians has led many female politicians to remain unmarried in the public eye.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Ahead of Elections, KMT Elders Outline Ten-Year Plan on Unification at Sun Yat-Sen Commemoration
content:
AT AN EVENT in Taipei on November 12th, organized by a number of senior KMT officials to commemorate the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, a ten-year plan for the political unification of Taiwan and China was set out. Over 250 individuals were in attendance at the event.

Given that the media cycle in Taiwan is focused on the upcoming local elections, there was relatively little attention to this news item. Nevertheless, among those in attendance at the event were former KMT Taipei mayoral candidate Ting Shou-chung, former KMT majority speaker Wang Jinpyng, and Su Chi, who is considered the architect of the 1992 Consensus. As such, a former premier, former Legislative Yuan head, former Examination Yuan head, and former legislators were among those in attendance.

The ten-year plan for the political unification of Taiwan and China was phrased as part of a “Cross-Strait Peace Initiative” with specific benchmarks. In 2027, a referendum to grant the government the power to conduct negotiations with China would be initiated by a KMT-controlled Legislative Yuan. In 2028, the KMT would return to power by winning the presidency. In 2030, market integration between Taiwan and China will occur. In 2032, a unified currency would be adopted between Taiwan and China. In 2036, discussions would be held on unification, which would include possibly adopting “One Country, Two Syste

author: Brian Hioe
title: New Taipei Mayoral Debate Revolves Around Infrastructure, Urban Needs
content:
THE NEW TAIPEI mayoral debate was held on November 13th. The race is between Su Chiao-hui of the DPP and Lee Shu-chuan of the KMT. Fringe candidate Su Hui-huang also participated in the debate, making outlandish suggestions unlikely to be adopted, such as allowing marriages involving multiple partners in order to solve the issue of Taiwan’s declining birthrate.

The debate between Su and Lee primarily revolved around infrastructure and New Taipei’s urban needs, with many New Taipei residents commuting to work elsewhere. As such, Lee doubled down on his career as an administrator and civil engineer, promising to reduce commute times. Lee also called for increased AI development in New Taipei, stating that New Taipei should strengthen links to the Beitou-Shilin Technology Park and Shezidao in Taipei. Lee positioned himself as building on the policy of his predecessors, Eric Chu and Hou You-yi. Lee also emphasized cooperation between himself and Chiang Wan-an in Taipei, stressing New Taipei’s links to Taipei infrastructure, such as the Taipei Dome.

Su Chiao-hui, in the meantime, emphasized residential policy. Su called for allowing New Taipei residents to live comfortably; young people should have more access to housing, while also allowing for cultural development, preserving heritage areas, developing tourism, and providing opportunities for young people. Su stressed her background as a New Taipei resident who was familiar with the different districts of New Taipei, and who would bring out the specificity of each area. Su also called for AI development for New Taipei, as well as suggested that New Taipei should form a special bureau in order to retain talent among civil servants, stating that this was an issue faced by New Taipei.

Apart from AI, urban renewal emerged as a common theme between the two candidates. Both candidates promised to implement urban renewal in a more streamlined manner, to keep pace with the demands of the city. All candidates, unsurprisingly, promised to quickly implement policy if elected.

A point of conflict between Su and Lee emerged regarding the central government’s role, as well as who would foot the bill for policy proposals. Su emphasized that she would put the needs of New Taipei residents first if it came to a conflict in imperatives between the central government and New Taipei, but that she could coordinate between the two sides. On the other hand, Lee sought to attack Su multiple times by claiming that she was unaware of where money for her policy proposals would come from. In response, Su cited that this would utilize higher tax revenue for New Taipei than in past years, but Lee still circled back to this point several times.

In closing, Su criticized the KMT for maintaining a negative campaign and attacking her family, seeing as she is the daughter of Premier Su Tseng-chang. Su stated that she could have focused attacks on Lee’s brother had she chosen, with Lee Shu-chuan’s brother Lee Szu-fu having been found guilty of extortion of tourism operators in Xiaoliuqiu earlier this year. Su then emphasized her campaign as forward-looking, seeking to establish a new future for New Taipei, but that this was a decision about the better choice for New Taipei, acknowledging where past KMT administrations of New Taipei had improved infrastructure.

Lee defended himself by stating that he viewed his brother as needing to face legal punishment. Lee also sought to defend himself against allegations he has increasingly faced about not declaring his assets or owning luxury properties, instead trying to emphasize that he was a regular person. Lee emphasized his past record as an administrator and stated that as a public servant, he was willing to face criticism. In his closing, then, Lee attempted to depict Su as not being of the people, circling around to this point several times, and attacking her past record as a legislator.

On the whole, Su’s debate performance was stronger than Lee due to better public speaking and debating skills. It is not for nothing that Lee has struggled in New Taipei despite that he otherwise should be in a more advantageous position after New Taipei was controlled by the KMT for two mayoral administrations, his poor campaigning skills have hindered him. Lee may have had a reputation as a competent administrator in the past, but he is not as skilled a politician. Nevertheless, he probably managed well enough in the debate that it will not have any significantly negative impact on voting.

New Taipei will be a hotly watched race going into the local elections, seeing as the race was already one in which Su seemed to possibly be doing better than Lee even before the “Ocean Current” phenomenon surged across Taiwan, impacting races across the country. Even if Shen were to be defeated in Taipei, it may actually be in New Taipei that the DPP has a chance to take northern Taiwanese territory traditionally controlled by the KMT.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Jensen Huang Scandal Likely to Serve as Pretext for Continued Chip Controls, Securitization
content:
NVIDIA FOUNDER Jensen Huang has suddenly come under scrutiny, with allegations that he was engaged in an affair with a purported Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Huang is an executive at a Singaporean data center company.

With Huang having now resigned from his position, Nvidia does not have a successor who can maintain the same public image. Still, most prognostications are that Nvidia’s role is bigger than simply Huang, and that the company will continue to grow.

Huang admitted to having an affair, something that has shattered his family man image in Taiwan. Huang is highly popular in Taiwan, probably due to his status as a returnee–seeing as he was born in Taiwan, but grew up in the US. Two other affairs by Huang later emerged, with other Nvidia executives.

A significant degree of media reporting on Huang usually focuses on when he visits night markets and other regular places during stints in Taiwan, as if to show that Huang–who was born in Taiwan but grew up in the US and has spent most of his life abroad–has maintained ties with his native land.

Huang’s background proves similar to that of many other Taiwanese tech entrepreneurs who, in fact, have spent most of their lives abroad. author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Making Hope Credible: Puma Shen and the Politics of Access in Taipei
content:
A HOME THAT can be renewed without repeated moves, a cultural allowance that continues into working adulthood, and an exercise service that comes to the neighbourhood: these are tangible reasons to pay attention to Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign for Taipei mayor. They also offer a way to test the comparison increasingly drawn between Shen and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. Beyond the excitement surrounding an unexpected challenger, what would make the city more accessible to people with unequal resources?

Shen’s command of municipal policy has helped change how voters see him. Nathan Batto’s account dated September 28 describes how detailed answers helped him reach beyond his established image as a specialist in civil defence and Chinese information warfare. His appeal invites scrutiny of what that expertise could deliver for residents who find existing services difficult to use.

THE COMPARISON reportedly helped shape the contest itself. ETtoday’s Tao Ben-he (³³¥»©M) reported on October 29 that President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) drew inspiration from Mamdani’s unexpected rise when insisting on Shen’s nomination as the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate. The reported connection poses a consequential question: if New York supplied inspiration for choosing a candidate, how much of Mamdani’s challenge to inequality has travelled with it?

Brian Hioe identified the distinction in New Bloom, also on October 29: Mamdani campaigned explicitly against socioeconomic inequality, while Shen has emphasised policy expertise and good governance. The proposals examined here suggest a distinctive contribution: reducing the practical burdens of using public provision. That could bring meaningful improvements, although its redistributive reach remains uneven, particularly where housing assistance depends on ownership.

Mamdani’s promises to freeze rents for rent-stabilised tenants, make buses free and provide universal childcare named household costs that government could reduce. His inaugural address on January 1 also connected childcare to taxing the wealthiest. Taipei need not reproduce those policies to learn from their political clarity: residents should understand whose circumstances will improve, who will contribute and what public authority will do.

Shen has offered a wide range of policy proposals. From that platform, I examine three areas—housing and urban renewal, cultural support for young adults, and neighbourhood exercise services for older residents—to assess how his proposals would change access to public resources. These examples reveal different relationships between administrative reform and inequality; they cannot establish the overall redistributive ambition of his platform.

HOUSING PROVIDES the hardest test. Taipei’s existing approach is not simply to leave residents to negotiate with developers. The city already promotes publicly led renewal and faster review through its urban renewal programmes. It also provides temporary accommodation and describes neighbourhood-based relocation as an objective, including arrangements involving social housing. Shen’s alternative must therefore demonstrate what it changes in practice.

His proposed circular urban renewal scheme (無限都更) changes the sequence of redevelopment. Willing owners would exchange existing property rights for a new home, or rights to use one, before their original site is rebuilt. The city would assemble an initial housing supply and manage the exchange; completed redevelopment would replenish resources for subsequent rounds. The objective is to avoid the familiar sequence of moving into temporary accommodation and moving again after reconstruction.

The scheme recognises disruption as a real cost, especially for older residents whose routines depend on nearby care and social relationships. It could make agreement easier without treating reluctant residents as obstacles. But Shen’s policy acknowledges limited initial supply. Its preference for nearby exchanges needs to be supported by identified sites and a realistic timetable.

Valuation is equally important. Shen’s scheme envisages settling differences between old and new property values, with loan assistance where needed. An older owner with little income may still struggle to bridge that difference. Independent valuations, accessible advice and safeguards against unaffordable debt would determine whether the exchange expands choice or mainly assists households already able to pay.

Property exchange also begins with ownership. Tenants cannot exchange an asset they do not own, and may remain exposed to displacement even when owners gain protection from repeated moves. Housing justice therefore requires affordable rental provision and safeguards for tenants affected by redevelopment.

Shen’s housing platform does address rental supply. It proposes using repair subsidies and tax incentives to bring approximately 4,000 underused homes into leasing and management arrangements, and obtaining additional social housing through renewal. However, Taipei already operates a government-backed leasing and management programme, whose current phase includes incentives for accessible accommodation for older tenants. The change is an expansion and reorientation of existing instruments, whose additional results need to be measurable.

Success should be measured by how many additional households secure suitable homes at sustainable rents, and for how long. Public resources also involve competing claims: allocating scarce homes to property exchanges has an opportunity cost for people waiting for affordable housing. Shen should explain those priorities alongside his plans to accelerate redevelopment.

HIS CULTURAL COIN proposal offers a more immediate and clearly defined extension. The national programme currently provides eligible 13- to 22-year-olds with 1,200 points annually, each worth NT$1, for approved cultural spending. Shen proposes a Taipei-funded extension covering ages 23 to 30 at the same annual amount. This would continue support after national eligibility ends, rather than increase the allowance for existing recipients.

Cultural participation need not cease to be a public concern when someone leaves education or starts work. Books, cinema and performance can become discretionary expenses for young adults meeting housing and employment costs. Continuing the allowance would make a modest portion of that spending a shared public responsibility.

The relevant test is whether the allowance brings additional people into cultural participation. A flat benefit may subsidise existing consumers more readily than it reaches people with little time, familiarity or confidence to participate. Outreach through workplaces and community organisations could help it reach beyond established audiences. Evaluation should therefore consider who begins attending or buying cultural work, alongside total spending.

Eligibility also matters. Young people may live, work or study in Taipei without sharing the same registration status. Clear rules would show whom the municipal extension includes and allow voters to consider exclusions they may not themselves encounter.

THE EXERCISE-BUS proposal addresses another barrier: distance. Shen proposes converting electric buses into mobile exercise classrooms, visiting community locations on regular schedules. Reported plans include professional coaching, fitness assessments, nutritional advice and health records. The service would bring supported activity closer to older residents rather than assume they can travel to a sports centre.

Taipei already offers older residents free access to swimming pools and gyms at district sports centres during designated hours, as its current provision shows. Bringing coached sessions into neighbourhoods could make that provision more useful to people deterred by the journey or unfamiliar equipment. The proposal’s contribution is to reduce the effort required to participate, complementing facilities that residents must travel to themselves.

A pilot could demonstrate that contribution by prioritising neighbourhoods poorly served by existing facilities and involving older residents in its design. Regular visits and consistent staffing would help turn an initial session into a sustained activity. Coordination with community providers should establish where a mobile service adds value, while evaluation should record whether it reaches people previously excluded, including those with limited mobility.

THE THREE EXAMPLES show why administrative reform can matter politically. Helping an older owner move with less disruption, continuing cultural support into adulthood and bringing coached exercise closer to home would expand practical choices. These gains deserve recognition on their own terms. Their limits are also specific: a property exchange cannot serve tenants directly, while an allowance or mobile service must reach beyond people already able to participate.

Delivery would require published budgets and a clear division of responsibility between Taipei and the national government. As the party holding the presidency, the DPP cannot treat national constraints as someone else’s problem. Progress should be measured against existing provision: additional affordable tenancies, new cultural participants and sustained exercise participation. Independent review should also record unsuccessful applications and complaints, making exclusion visible alongside headline results.

Residents should help determine those standards. Housing exchanges require independent advice and meaningful consent. Cultural policy should hear from young people who rarely enter established venues, and exercise services from older residents absent from organised activities. Their experience can reveal whether a programme removes an obstacle or simply relocates it. Participation gives the people affected some influence over how success is defined.

Matthew d’Ancona’s article in The New World on October 21 distinguishes hope from confidence in inevitable progress; James Ball, published in The New World on September 28 stresses visible improvements. Together, they suggest a useful standard for Taipei: hope requires both a commitment to act and evidence that action changes people’s circumstances.

The reported Mamdani connection is therefore illuminating without making Shen a Taiwanese equivalent. In these selected policies, Shen’s promise is a more active municipal government that helps residents use resources already available and extends provision where gaps remain. That is a credible basis for reform. A broader challenge to urban inequality would also require explicit choices about who pays, whose housing claims take priority and how people without assets gain security.

The campaign’s democratic significance lies in making those choices open to public judgement. Clear commitments would give residents something to defend, contest and improve after November 28, whoever wins. Shen has offered practical reasons to believe that government could make city life easier. Making that hope durable means giving residents greater influence over the resources and decisions that shape their lives.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Unnamed Military Exercises Aim to Intimidate Taiwan Ahead of Elections, While Avoiding International Outcry
content:
ACCORDING TO TAIWANESE Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo, China is currently engaged in area access denial drills around Taiwan.

Such drills involve more than 100 naval and coast guard ships operating in waters around Taiwan. These exercises include the deployment of the Liaoning, China’s first aircraft carrier, and its carrier group.

Last week, on November 3rd, images of Chinese naval vessels deployed around Taiwan were released by National Security Council head Joseph Wu. Wu also drew attention to a large number of air sorties that had taken place on November 3rd, with 49 sorties of Chinese aircraft that entered Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone and crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait.

Previously, news reports had indicated that China may have been practicing for a potential blockade of Taiwan in late October and early November, through exercises that coordinated between its eastern, northern, and southern theater commands. According to national security officials, these drills were larger than previously named large-scale drills by China, such as the 2025 Justice Mission.

Indeed, it is notable that China has not formally announced any military drills to date. China normally conducts at least two named large-scale military exercises per year, in the spring and the fall. This has not occurred this year yet, though it might be expected that China w

author: Brian Hioe
title: Ahead of Elections, China Turns on Diplomatic Pressure on Taiwan in Lithuania, Pakistan, and Papua New Guinea
content:
THE TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT has announced that Taiwan will soon close its diplomatic office in Papua New Guinea. This occurs after the country set a deadline for all Taiwanese diplomatic staff to leave the country. As Taiwan does not officially have diplomatic relations with Papua New Guinea, the office is technically not an embassy, but a representative office.

The announcement was made unilaterally by Papua New Guinea in July. In response, Taiwan stated that it would suspend purchases of liquefied natural gas from Papua New Guinea, and that it would be shutting down its representative office.

It is unclear whether the move occurs at Papua New Guinea’s initiative or if it is a move aimed at shoring up ties with China. This, too, has been questioned in other incidents in which countries abruptly announced the downgrading of diplomatic representation by Taiwan or other measures, such as revoking overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines.

Indeed, in the past month, Pakistan announced that it would be revoking overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines EVA Air and China Airlines, before later reversing course on the move. It, too, is unclear whether the move occurred at Pakistan’s initiative, perhaps as a means of signalling alignment with China, or if China’s will led to the act–as well as why Pakistan reversed course.

It, too, is possible that international pressure led Pa
sourceTags: international pressure on Taiwan by China

author: Brian Hioe
title: May Chin Indictment Gestures Toward Extensive Reach of Chinese United Front Work
content:
INDEPENDENT PAN-BLUE legislator Kao Chin Su Mei, also known as May Chin or Ciwas Ali, and who is an Indigenous legislator of the Atayal people, has been indicted for Chinese United Front work. According to prosecutors, Chin accepted more than 170 million NTD, which was funneled to organizations, relatives, and other bodies in order to conduct influence operations aimed at winning elections. Prosecutors are seeking 14 years for Chin, who was previously facing charges about illegally importing Chinese COVID-19 vaccines for distribution among her constituents.

The networks of these organizations were managed by her office director, Chang Chun-chieh, and legislative assistants Chen Chih-huang and Lin Yi-chun. Chang is currently under investigation for having fled overseas by boat in order to avoid arrest, with authorities conducting raids earlier this month to find the vessel on which he escaped. Chang and Chen reportedly coordinated United Front efforts, while Lin acted as an intermediary with China. Chin has been accused of using her influence as a legislator in order to influence government policy in arms sales, defense, cross-strait relations, and international relations.

For her part, Chin has denied participation in such United Front work, suggesting that she did not need Chinese support to win elections. Chin also raised questions about why she was apparently under surveil

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: “My Body Is My Own”: Collective Memory, Remembrance, and Dignity in Taiwan Transgender and Intersex History
content:
This article submission was originally published by 跨服TransServer’s trans co-created column, Trans Day Reader and is syndicated here on New Bloom Magazine’s website with 跨服TransServer’s permission. In the original article, TransServer writes the following introduction:

November is Transgender Awareness Month and November 8th is Intersex Day of Remembrance. For the author, November 8th carries the weight of intertwined histories of medical violence within transgender and intersex communities, as well as the responsibility of building solidarity across these communities. Choosing this day to begin HRT, Yo-Ling offers this Trans Day Reader as an act of intervention, grounding its significance within the Taiwanese context.

The medical establishment profoundly impacts intersex well-being, as medical authority often overshadows bodily autonomy for intersex people. At the same time, scholars shape collective memory by ghostwriting for historical subjects. Positioned with critique and reflexivity, this article revisits archives of Mr. Xie Jianshun’s gender transition under duress, but more importantly, his acts of resistance, which advance a politics of self-respect for Sinophone trans and intersex communities. In reaching a wider public, readers must recognize academic critique as an autonomous domain and respect the author’s embodied self-disclosure.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: 「我的身體為我自己所有」：台灣跨性別與雙性人歷史中的集體記憶、紀念及尊嚴
content:
本篇投稿原刊於跨服TransServer之《跨日典》跨性別共創欄目，在此以《破土雜誌》官網做轉載。在原文中，跨服撰寫了本篇以下的引言：

每年11月是跨性別意識月，11月8日作爲紀念閒性人的日子，承載著跨性別與間性人/雙性人社群所經歷醫療暴力歷史的重量，同時也肩負著在這些社群之間建立團結的責任。有靈選擇這天開始用藥，以此紀念辭作為行動，也賦予其台灣語境的意涵。

醫療體制深刻影響著間性人/雙性人福祉，醫療權威蔓延至個體身體改造之決策，相關學者更進一步透過代筆當事人塑造集體記憶。本文帶著批判與反身性現身，重述謝尖順先生被迫進行性別轉換的檔案及其主體抗爭，向華語跨性別與雙性人社群發出自我尊重的倡議。本文面向廣泛社群的同時，讀者亦須理解學術批判作為獨立疆域的本質，並尊重作者的現身。

11月8日，既是我性別肯認荷爾蒙治療的用藥週年紀念日，又是雙性人紀念日。選擇這個日期開始用藥，有它背後的故事和政治原因。我是一名台灣跨性別倡議者，也是一名從事跨性別研究和台灣戰後跨性別歷史研究的獨立學者。台灣首例使用荷爾蒙進行性別轉換的記載來自於1950年代，且該案例與「性別肯認」相去甚遠。祝願這篇《跨日典》的篇章能提醒我們所有人：守護我們的集體記憶本身就是一種抵抗，尤其是當我們的歷史被一群消費我們的受苦、扭曲並複製醫療與檔案暴力現實，以至損害華語世界跨性別與雙性人集體尊嚴的學者書寫時。

1953年8月14日，台南陸軍第518醫院的醫師們發現，一名名為謝尖順的士兵具有雙性人特徵。醫師們於8月20日進行剖腹探查手術，以確定謝尖順所謂真正的「生理性別」，並判定其解剖結構屬「女性」，因他擁有子宮、兩側卵巢及輸卵管。隨後，醫師們決定，謝尖順該接受「變性」療程，包括後續手術及女性化荷爾蒙治療，以使他成為女性。[1] 期間謝尖順強烈表達了希望繼續以男性身份生活的堅持，甚至在8月21日剖腹探查手術後，向記者表示：「過了卅六個年頭的男子生活，再叫我變成一位女性，那麼我非要自殺不可」（《聯合日報》，1953年8月21日）。關於謝先生性別轉換的檔案資料一貫顯示，他始終將自己視為男性，並對被錯稱為女性以及經醫療介入「被變性」為女性感到極度不適。

1953年稍晚，謝先生接到命令，須從台南的第518醫院轉院至台北的陸海空軍第一總醫院接受進一步「變性」醫療處置，他向記者表示：「我的主張已經決定不上臺北。誰要我去，莫如送我兩粒花生米 (即兩粒子彈的意思)。我寧死不屈。我雖有軍人身分，以服從為天職，但我的身體為我自己所有。我有處理我自己身體之自由」（《民聲日報》，1953年12月9日）。然而，儘管他明確拒絕，仍於1954年初被轉送至台北，繼續接受「治療」。

1955年秋季，第一總醫院的醫師們，為了讓謝先生「能夠做母親」、「便 [他] 的月紅如一般的女性一樣」，並「為了在醫術研究上獲得更偉大的成就」，擅自專購雌激素注射劑給謝先生做實驗（《聯合日報》，1955年10月15日）。關於對注射雌激素的感受，記者訪問謝先生時，報導記載：「針插在體內的痛苦還在其次，眼看自己的身體，一天一天地在起變化， [他] 實在有點躭心」（《聯合日報》，1955年10月17日）。在1950年代台灣軍醫院體系的「照護」下，身為一名士兵，謝先生只能接受當局對其身體所施加的一切，並在那些微小卻充滿力量的時刻，依據他對自身身為男性的認知
sourceTags: 台灣跨性別與雙性人歷史

author: Brian Hioe
title: The Country That Has Forgotten Joshua Wong
content:
THE SENTENCING of Hong Kong political activist Joshua Wong to an additional ten years in prison, on top of the time that he was already serving, should be a stark warning to Taiwan of the future that it faces if it acquiesces to Chinese political control. Still, one notes that many in Taiwan have forgotten the lessons of Hong Kong.

Wong’s extra ten years in jail were on the basis of alleged collusion with foreign forces. Wong has already spent six years in prison and recently celebrated his 30th birthday behind bars. The new charges mean that by the time Wong gets out of jail, he will be 40. Wong pled guilty to the charges, not because they are true, but as a means to lower his jail sentence.

This proves a tragic fate for Wong, who rose to fame as a youth activist as a teenager. In another future, as one of Hong Kong’s best and brightest, Wong would have taken up leadership in Hong Kong society. Instead, the society that Wong has sacrificed so much for has, because of Chinese political control, locked him away.

Clearly, through locking him away, China aims to hope that the world forgets about his plight, as well as that of many other Hongkongers who are not as internationally well-known as he. Nevertheless, many in Taiwan have already forgotten, or have come to see Hong Kong as a faraway place that offers few lessons for Taiwan.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Do the US Midterms Mean for Taiwan?
content:
THE US MIDTERM elections resulted in a massive win for Democrats, who made historic gains and took control of both the House and Senate. Consequently, the win has been interpreted as a rebuke to Donald Trump’s presidency.

For its part, the Taiwanese government has sought to reassure that support for Taiwan is bipartisan and that it expects arms sales to continue. Nevertheless, one notes that Trump has himself suspended arms sales, out of an apparent desire to please Chinese president Xi Jinping in trade negotiations.

Analysts have suggested that Trump’s actions may be further constrained after the midterms. After all, Trump is now a lame duck, with two years left in his term. His ability to accomplish his agenda will become further limited with the House and Senate out of his control.

At the same time, Trump may seek to override institutions altogether, tapping into his base. Trump supporters were willing to invade the Capitol as part of an attempted insurrection on January 6, 2021, as part of an attempt to prevent the certification of the 2020 presidential election won by Joe Biden, and they may do so again.

It would not be out of character for Trump to try and dismantle institutions he views as opposed to him. If pushed into a corner and desperate, it is unclear what Trump or his supporters may attempt. Trump will be reaching the end of his second term, but Trump has sugg

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Does the Taipei Mayoral Debate Tell Us?
content:
THE TAIPEI MAYORAL DEBATE occurred on October 31st, after much discussion ahead of time about whether Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an would be willing to participate. The Shen campaign clamored for a debate, seeing as Shen’s strengths were seen in public speaking and debating, while Chiang is known for sometimes being a stiff public speaker.

The controversy about a police raid on Commander D, a gay bar in Ximending, added to such speculation. Namely, with Chiang stating that he would still attend Pride after the controversy following the raid, the debate was scheduled on the same day as Pride. That Chiang suspended a day of campaigning due to poor health prior to Pride and the debate stoked further speculation. Still, in the end, Chiang appeared at the debate without issue.

Few new policy proposals were made at the debate, which instead was primarily an opportunity for the two candidates to criticize each other and to craft their political images. Shen doubled down on efforts to depict himself as a candidate who is knowledgeable about policy, has a firm grasp of data, and has a vision for Taipei governance. By contrast, Chiang mostly touted the accomplishments of his mayoral administration, and suggested that Shen lacked knowledge of what the Taipei city government was already doing.

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RS

author: Brian Hioe
title: Endangered Eastern Grass Owl Habitat Threatened by Shalun Science Park
content:
ENVIRONMENTALISTS HAVE warned of the potential displacement of the Eastern grass owl as a result of the construction of the Shalun Science Park.

The Eastern grass owl is a critically endangered species in Taiwan, with its habitat including Tainan, Chiayi, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and it is Taiwan’s only owl species that nests in grasslands. After much effort by environmentalists to rebuild its habitat on the Dadu Mountain Plateau, the Eastern grass owl was found to have returned to central Taiwan earlier this year. It is thought that the Eastern grass owl disappeared from central Taiwan in the 1960s.

Environmentalists voiced concerns about the owl’s habitat at the second-stage environmental impact review, whose scoping session concluded on October 12th. The planned development zones “Parking 1” and “Industrial 1-2” would threaten the habitat of the Eastern grass owl, in that the current area is considered top-tier nesting grounds for the owl. As such, developers were urged to create habitats for the Eastern grass owl before construction. The Kaohsiung Science Park has been cited as an example of where development has already displaced the Eastern grass owl.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Migrant Rights Remain Unheard Ahead of Election
content:
THE KUAI KUAI STRIKE that came to an end earlier this month involved migrant workers being led across picket lines by labor brokers. Migrant workers were instructed to say on video that they were willing to work, unlike striking Kuai Kuai workers.

The strike by workers at iconic snack Kuai Kuai’s Zhongli factory came to an end after five days earlier this month. Kuai Kuai is an iconic snack best known for a superstition that keeping bags of it near machinery keeps them running smoothly. Kuai Kuai operates one factory in Taoyuan, but 130 out of 155 union members voted in favor of a strike after the company decided to relocate to Hsinchu.

The two sites are 39 kilometers from each other, meaning that the move is untenable for many workers. Workers were only informed of the land scale on September 1st. The factory has operated in Zhongli since 1968, and 1/3rd of workers at Kuai Kuai have worked there for more than thirty years, despite the fact that their wages are near minimum wage.

Workers have accused the San-Ti Group that owns Kuai Kuai of perhaps having only acquired the company with an eye on selling its land to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. Originally, Kuai Kuai workers were only offered a 5% pay increase and verbal assurances that they would be relocated to the new factory. author: Brian Hioe
title: Pakistan Abruptly Cancels Taiwanese Overflight Routes Then Reverses Course
content:
IN AN UNUSUAL series of events, in short order, Pakistan declared that Taiwanese airlines would not be allowed to fly over the country, then reversed course on the decision.

The decision was announced by Pakistan’s Minister of Defense Khawaja Asif, who stated that the new policy was made to comply with Pakistan’s One China Policy. Originally, Taiwanese airlines EVA Air and China Airlines had been cleared for overflight privileges by Pakistan from October 28 of this year through March 27, 2027, as approved by the country’s Civil Aviation Authority.

This would be the first time that a country has revoked overflight privileges for Taiwanese air carriers, on the basis of a claimed One China Policy. If so, it could be that Pakistan would be seeking closer ties with China, and hitting out at Taiwan would be a means of doing so. Or Pakistan could have been acting on China’s behest, with China expected to try and constrain Taiwan’s international space ahead of the upcoming local elections next month. As for why Pakistan later reversed course, this is also unclear, except perhaps that international backlash was larger than expected–or perhaps there was pressure behind the scenes from the US.

author: Brian Hioe
title: China Steps Up Transnational Repression Ahead of Elections
content:
CHINA HAS STEPPED up efforts to intimidate Taiwan ahead of elections in November. This has occurred with the usual combination of domestic threats and military exercises. Nevertheless, one can point to a discernible effort to project power over Taiwan.

In particular, China released high-resolution satellite images of Taiwan, as well as a propaganda poster, on the anniversary of the handover of Taiwan from Japanese to ROC control.

The satellite imagery was designed to convey a sense of having already penetrated Taiwan, such that it can observe Taiwan easily from without–and to contribute to the sense that the Chinese military could take Taiwan at any time. To this extent, as with any display of Chinese military hardware, this would also be signalling between the two militaries, with the Chinese government showing its capacities to the ROC military as a means of intimidation.

One can perceive attacks that have occurred in Taiwan in recent memory as similarly aimed at projecting power. News broke earlier this month of the indictment of five men over a plot to hit stand-up comic Huang Yi-hao with a car, in retribution for a comedy show in which Huang mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Explains the Rise of Puma Shen as a DPP Candidate in Taipei?
content:
THE METEORIC RISE of Puma Shen as the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate has made what was previously perceived as a relatively slow election into an unpredictable and exciting one. It is generally expected that Shen, whether or not he wins the Taipei mayorship, could be the best-performing DPP Taipei mayoral candidate since Chen Shui-bian in 1992–Chen, of course, later became president.

Shen being sent to run in Taipei was originally perceived as his being sent there as a sacrificial candidate. After all, Shen was previously mainly known for tough stances on China, as the founder of the Doublethink Lab, which researches Chinese disinformation, and of the Kuma Academy, Taiwan’s best-known civil defense organization. It would be expected that he would struggle in historically pan-Blue Taipei. Running Shen, then, would be to field a younger and untested candidate for Taipei, whereas running another post-Sunflower politician, such as Enoch Wu, who had previously contested Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an unsuccessfully, would have been seen as putting little effort into the race. Shen, as a party list legislator, had never had to run an electoral campaign before.
